Cracks appearing across walls, doors suddenly refusing to close and windows becoming difficult to open are emerging as a new concern for homeowners in London after an unusually hot and dry summer. The problem is linked to subsidence, as heat and prolonged dry conditions cause the clay-rich soil beneath homes to shrink and shift.
London and parts of southeast England are particularly vulnerable because much of the region is built on clay. When the soil is wet, clay absorbs water and expands. During hot, dry periods, it loses moisture and contracts. If this movement happens unevenly beneath a building, its foundations can shift, causing cracks and other structural problems.
The process is known as “shrink-swell”. It becomes particularly significant when the ground beneath different parts of a property moves at different rates.
“Subsidence is one of the most damaging geohazards in the UK today,” a spokesperson for the British Geological Survey said, as quoted by CNN.
Making the problem worse
High temperatures are not the only factor. Trees and other vegetation can also contribute to ground movement. During dry conditions, their roots extend deeper into the soil in search of water, drawing moisture from the ground around nearby properties.
This can further dry out the clay and cause it to contract.
Older homes can be more exposed because they often have shallower foundations. More than half of London's homes were built before 1945, making the city's ageing housing stock an important factor in the risk.
The problem is also spreading beyond London and southeast England.
“When I started in the business 40 years ago, it was mostly a London and southeast England issue. But with climate change it is now affecting many other parts of the UK as well,” said subsidence expert Bob Gibson, director of Building & Structural Consultants.
Every hot, dry summer can trigger a surge in subsidence claims. In 2025, the UK insurance industry paid out a record $415 million in subsidence-related claims, up 10% from the previous year, according to the Association of British Insurers.
The pressure has continued this year. Insurers paid more than $97 million in subsidence-related claims in the second quarter of 2026, while the average claim rose to a record $27,000.
“Following the extremely hot and dry weather we saw over July and August this year, it’s likely we’ll see more subsidence claims over the coming months,” said Louise Clark, general insurance policy manager at the ABI.
What does subsidence mean for homeowners?
Subsidence does not necessarily mean a house is about to collapse. But it can cause serious and expensive damage, including cracks in walls, distorted door and window frames and problems with foundations.
The extent of the damage depends on both the underlying ground conditions and how vulnerable the building is.
“There are two ingredients to consider in subsidence risk,” said Brunella Balzano, senior lecturer in structural design at Cardiff University. “The vulnerability of the building and the hazard itself.”
Homeowners may have limited options for addressing the underlying ground movement. Measures can include removing trees or vegetation close to the property, installing barriers to prevent roots from reaching the foundations and, in more severe cases, underpinning the building by strengthening or extending its foundations.
But the growing risk is also creating a problem for the property insurance market.
“I think it’s possible … that in the near future, subsidence might not be insured anymore,” Balzano said.
Homeowners in high-risk areas are already reporting difficulties obtaining cover. Gibson said insurers were “jacking-up premiums hugely, or not inviting renewal of subsidence cover”.
That creates another property-market concern: serious subsidence can reduce a home's value, make it harder to sell and leave owners facing substantial repair costs.
London's particular vulnerability comes from the type of clay beneath much of the city. Some of these soils contain expansive minerals that respond strongly to changes in moisture.
That means a combination of prolonged heat, drought and vegetation can produce ground movement beneath buildings.
The risk is expected to increase as temperatures rise. British Geological Survey data indicates that more than 26% of properties in London could be affected by subsidence by 2070 if global warming continues at roughly its current pace.
For homeowners, the warning signs can therefore be more than cosmetic. New or widening cracks, sticking doors and distorted windows can indicate movement in the building and may warrant a professional assessment.
Subsidence is generally a gradual process rather than an immediate threat to life. But as extreme heat and drought become more frequent, ground movement is becoming an increasingly important consideration for Britain's housing stock, insurance costs and property values.

CHENNAI: The city’s informal workers are losing both working days and income due to heat-related illness, with 28.4% of workers surveyed in Vyasarpadi reporting that they had lost at least one working day because of heat-related illness, a community-led study has found.
The study, which surveyed 260 residents in Vyasarpadi and Ramapuram between the last week of June and the first week of August 2026, highlighted the growing impact of prolonged heat exposure on the health and livelihoods of vulnerable communities.
The economic impact was evident in the experience of Chinnayya, who has been running a tiffin shop in Ramapuram for 34 years. Prolonged exposure to heat while working near a stove, along with other difficulties, affected his health and forced him to shut his shop for more than two months. He spent around Rs 60,000 on treatment and estimated that he lost nearly Rs 3 lakh in income. For four months, he could operate his shop only at night.
In Vyasarpadi, 28.4% of workers said that they had lost at least one working day due to heat-related illness, with some reporting losses of up to six days. In Ramapuram, 16.9% reported losing working days, with some cases involving losses of up to 15 days.
Working conditions further increased workers’ vulnerability. In Vyasarpadi, 38.8% of workers said they had no shade at their workplace, while 44.8% said they did not get afternoon breaks. Another 37.3% reported that free drinking water was unavailable at their workplace.
The health burden was also significant. Nearly 94.7% of respondents in Vyasarpadi reported dehydration or excessive thirst in the previous 30 days, while 78.2% reported headaches and 68.4% exhaustion. Muscle cramps were reported by 57.1%, while 51.1% reported dizziness or fainting.
Heat-related hospitalisation was reported by 38.3% of households in Vyasarpadi during the previous 30 days, compared with 21.3% in Ramapuram.
For many informal workers, following official heat advisories is difficult as the recommendation to remain indoors and avoid outdoor activity during peak afternoon hours conflicts with the need to earn a daily income.
The study also found gaps in awareness about heatwave preparedness. About 75.2% of respondents in Vyasarpadi said they did not know which government department to contact during a heat emergency.
Further, 73.7% said they had either not received heatwave warnings or did not know whether they had received them in May 2026.
Small businesses also reported losses during periods of extreme heat. Flower shop owner Indra said, “On some days, I purchase flowers worth Rs 1,500 but manage to sell only around Rs 500 worth of stock.”
Hot Chips shop owner Kumaresan said, “The heat between 10 am and noon makes it difficult to remain inside the shop, but closing the shop is not an option.”
The report called for shaded and ventilated rest spaces, free drinking water, compulsory rest breaks during extreme heat and compensation for heat-related loss of work. It also sought more public drinking water points, heat-resilient bus stops and better access to public toilets.

Say Goodbye To Neckfans: China Rolls Out Air Conditioning Vests For Workers During Heatwave
Being outside, let alone working outside, in intense heat can lead to heat stroke and heat exhaustion. Employees who work outdoors in the summertime doing maintenance such as yard work, road construction, and sanitation are prone to developing heat exhaustion as they spend hours beneath the sweltering sun. Now, one Chinese company has developed a solution to help keep workers cool.
Sanitation workers in Nanjing, China, are continuing their work with the help of a cooling vest. Instead of bringing a portable neck fan or using another tool to stay cool, workers wear the device as a vest. It features two built-in mini fans that provide continuous airflow as the workers spend their shift in the summer heat. The device is being used during China's Sanfu season, the country's hottest days of the year. The vests are designed to work for multiple hours at a time, ensuring that workers have enough cool air to get through a morning and afternoon shift.
The cooling garments are specifically built to help sanitation workers avoid heat-related illness and heat stroke. Reports show that thousands of workers experience heat-related illnesses due to heat exposure, many of which are fatal. Cooling vests are one step toward preventing illness and potential fatalities among outdoor workers. They're a great way to stay cool in the summer heat.
How these air conditioning vests work
At first glance, the cooling vests resemble a standard orange reflective uniform you may see road crews wearing. Upon closer inspection, the vests contain two mini fans near the midsection of the device. The fans have three speeds to control how much power each produces. It works like a ceiling fan: higher speeds move more air, and lower settings move less. No matter the setting, the fans circulate air inside the vest, spreading it throughout the body and cooling the wearer. The fans are powered by compact rechargeable battery packs that last up to four hours and can be recharged on a lunch break, after which they can be used for another four hours.
Workers who have tried out the cooling vests say they felt cool air blowing around their body. They are also built with low-noise fans so workers don't have to hear a whirring fan while doing their jobs. The vests are not only being worn by sanitation workers, as the urban management department is marketing them citywide in Nanjing. Soon, it may even spread nationwide as it becomes more popular.
There is more than one kind of cooling vest
This cooling vest isn't the only one out there, as other innovative cooling tech is also being put to good use. Other types of cooling vests use different mechanisms to cool down the wearer. Evaporative cooling vests use gel-like material that captures and holds moisture inside them. They are dunked into freezing water before being worn. Once on, they use heat to evaporate the gel and water to cool down the wearer. Phase change cooling vests – like ones in Changzhou of Jiangsu Province – use frozen cooling packs that are placed in pockets inside the vest to help sanitation workers. Passive cooling vests and Hybrid cooling vests work similarly, while Liquid cooling vests include channels for chilled water to run through.
If you plan to work outside and need a way to cool down, you can try wearable cooling devices. You can take cooling vests, fans, and misters with you. Whether you're on the job, doing a bit of yard work, enjoying an outdoor event or playing a sport, there are tools you can use to help you keep cool.

Mumbai rains: Waterlogging disrupts travel as IMD issues yellow alert
More rain expected in Mumbai and nearby areas on Monday, says weather department
Continuous heavy rainfall since Saturday night has disrupted normal life across Mumbai and adjoining areas, with widespread waterlogging reported on roads and railway tracks, causing difficulties for commuters and motorists.
In Nalasopara, severe waterlogging was reported on the eastern side of Nalasopara Railway Station, forcing passengers to wade through accumulated water to reach the station and nearby areas. Heavy crowds were also seen inside the station premises as persistent rain disrupted movement.
Several parts of Vasai-Virar have also been affected by the downpour. Roads around Centre Park and Tulinj Bridge in Nalasopara were waterlogged, creating difficulties for motorists and pedestrians during the morning hours.
In Mumbai, heavy rain in Dadar added to commuter woes, while railway tracks at Kurla station were flooded following the prolonged spell of rainfall. The waterlogging raised concerns over movement around key suburban railway stations as the city continued to receive rain.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued a yellow alert for Mumbai, Thane and Palghar, forecasting thunderstorms, lightning, moderate rainfall and strong winds of 40-50 kmph in some areas. Isolated pockets could also receive heavy rainfall.
The weather department has forecast generally cloudy conditions over Mumbai, with intermittent moderate rain or thundershowers likely. The combination of continued rainfall and waterlogging could further affect road and rail movement, particularly in low-lying areas.
Rainfall activity is expected to continue over Mumbai and neighbouring areas in the coming days, with further showers forecast for Monday.
The spell of rain comes as Mumbai enters the Ganesh festival period, when movement across the city increases significantly. With Ganesh idol immersion processions scheduled to begin from Tuesday, continued rainfall could add to traffic and logistical challenges for commuters, devotees and civic authorities.
With more rain expected, residents in vulnerable and waterlogging-prone areas are likely to face continued disruption as authorities monitor the situation and weather conditions across the Mumbai Metropolitan Region.
With IANS inputs

Mumbai Rain Alert: Heavy Rain in Mumbai-Thane on the Eve of Ganesh Chaturthi; Yellow Alert for 8 Districts, Warning of Stormy Winds
Mumbai News: Rain has made a strong presence since last night in Mumbai and its suburbs. Intense rain has been ongoing in Mulund, Thane, Kalwa, Mumbra, and Diva areas since midnight. In Navi Mumbai, the rain continues, marking the arrival of rain in the city and suburbs on the eve of Ganesh Chaturthi. After a few days of respite, the intensity of rain has increased again since September 12.
15 Millimeters of Rain Recorded by Early Morning
The weather department reported that approximately 15 millimeters of rain was recorded by 5 AM in the Mulund and Thane areas. The ongoing rain has made many roads wet, causing citizens to face the rain during the morning hours. With significant crowds in markets and public places due to the Ganesh Festival, the rain has made its presence felt.
Yellow Alert for 8 Districts Including Mumbai
The Indian Meteorological Department's Mumbai center issued a Yellow Alert at 7 AM for the next 3 hours. Light to moderate rain along with thunderstorm activity is expected in some areas of 8 districts including Mumbai, Palghar, Thane, Raigad, Pune, Nashik, Dhule, and Jalgaon. There is also a possibility of lightning with thunder in some areas.
Warning of Strong Winds with Thunder
The weather department has indicated that winds of 30 to 40 kilometers per hour may blow in some areas along with the rain. Citizens are advised to take necessary precautions. Especially on the eve of Ganesh Festival, the increased rainfall may impact pandals, decorations, and the movements of devotees. Given the current rain situation in Mumbai and its suburbs, both the administration and citizens need to remain alert.

Temperatures could reach 44°C in parts of Morocco through Monday, Sept. 14, while strong winds are expected in the north Sunday, the General Directorate of Meteorology said in an updated orange alert.
Highs of 40°C to 44°C are forecast Sunday and Monday in provinces including Marrakech, Fez, Beni Mellal, Kenitra, Settat, Taroudant and Tata.
Temperatures of 36°C to 40°C are expected in areas including Casablanca, Rabat, Salé, Meknes, Agadir, Essaouira, Safi and El Jadida during the same period.
The bulletin also forecasts highs of 38°C to 41°C in Tan-Tan, Oued Ed Dahab, Boujdour, Laayoune and Tarfaya.
Separately, wind gusts of 75 to 85 kilometers per hour are expected Sunday, Sept. 13, in Fahs-Anjra and Tangier-Assilah. Both the heat and wind warnings were classified at the orange vigilance level in the bulletin issued Sunday morning.
